about.title: Claremont Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Claremont's tree-lined streets and Village shops draw plenty of foot traffic, but wet floors, cracked walkways, poor lighting, and uneven parking lots can turn a routine errand into a serious injury. Whether it happened at a store along Indian Hill Boulevard, an apartment complex near the Colleges, or a business off Foothill Boulevard, California law requires the property owner to have known, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard before you're able to hold them accountable. That's why acting quickly matters: surveillance footage often gets erased within days, and the physical evidence of a spill or broken step can disappear fast. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves, but we can connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney in our network who understands how Los Angeles County premises cases work and can help you sort out what happened and what it might be worth.

whyChoose.title: Why Notice and Evidence Matter in a Claremont Fall Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California premises law hinges on notice, so an attorney can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records showing the hazard existed long enough for someone to have caught it.

items.title: Preserving Video Before It's Overwritten
items.desc: Many Claremont stores and apartment complexes recycle surveillance footage within days or weeks, so requesting preservation letters quickly can be the difference between having proof and having nothing.

items.title: Navigating Comparative Fault and Your Deadline
items.desc: Because California follows pure comparative fault, even a partial share of blame doesn't bar recovery, but you generally have two years to act (less if a government-owned property is involved), so timing your claim right matters.

items.question: I fell in a store near the Claremont Village. What should I do first?
items.answer: Try to photograph the exact spot, including any spill, debris, or lighting issue, before it gets cleaned up or fixed. Report the fall to management and ask that they preserve any surveillance video. Getting a written incident report and seeking medical attention, even if you feel okay, can also help document what happened.

items.question: What if the property owner says I wasn't watching where I was walking?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still recover damages even if you're found partly responsible, though your share of fault would reduce the amount. An independent attorney can help push back on unfair blame-shifting and look at the full picture, including whether the hazard should have been fixed or marked.

items.question: How long do I have to file a claim if I fell at a Claremont city park or public building?
items.answer: Claims against public entities, including the City of Claremont, have much shorter deadlines than the general two-year window, sometimes just six months to file a government claim. If a public property is involved, it's worth getting connected with an attorney as soon as possible so that deadline isn't missed.
